title: Why do seasons exist on other planets?
subtitle: Planets & orbits
subject: sciences
description: On Earth, the seasons come from the tilt of the axis. Elsewhere, this same principle gives winters of 42 years… or almost no season at all.

hero.hook: Our four seasons are a moderate case. Elsewhere, a summer can last for decades.

blocks.text: On Earth, summer and winter arise mainly from the **inclination** of the axis: approximately **23.5°**. The Sun hits harder on one hemisphere, then the other. This model seems obvious. In the Solar System, it is rather a moderate version.
Each planet combines its inclination and the shape of its orbit. Result: worlds without seasons, others with extreme contrasts, and winters that last for decades.
The  is the angle between the axis of rotation of a planet and the perpendicular to its orbit. The larger it is, the more marked the seasons. [[Obliquity]]

blocks.caption: Uranus, tilted at about 98°, experiences extreme seasons lasting 42 years.

blocks.text: **Uranus** is the extreme case: inclination of approximately **98°**, almost lying down. It takes **84 years** to go around the Sun. Each pole then receives nearly **42 years** of continuous day, then **42 years** of total night. **March**, at **25.2°**, resembles Earth, but its year lasts **687 terrestrial days**: spring and autumn of six months. **Jupiter** and **Mercury**, almost straight, have almost no seasons.
On Uranus and Neptune, extreme pressures could “rain” diamonds formed from atmospheric carbon.

sections.title: When the distance from the Sun also matters

blocks.text: On Earth, the orbit is almost circular: the distance from the Sun varies little. It is therefore not what makes summer or winter, but the angle of the rays.

On **March**, the orbit is much more oval, more **eccentric**: from **207 to 249 million km**. In the Southern Hemisphere, summer falls near , the closest point to the Sun. Shorter, but warmer summers. This thermal shock sometimes triggers planetary **** dust storms that obscure the sky. [[<perihelion>]]
In **2018**, a seasonal Martian storm permanently stopped the Opportunity rover by blocking the Sun.

**Mercury**, without real atmosphere or inclination, lives mainly in daily **** extremes: **430 °C** in the Sun, **-180 °C** at night. **Venus** rotates in reverse, in  from east to west, with extreme tilt, but its monstrous **greenhouse effect traps heat in the atmosphere and equalizes the temperature towards **Z460** °C** everywhere, all the time. **Saturn**, tilted like the Earth, has seasons of about **7 years**. The angle of the  changes the light received by each hemisphere and even changes the color of the clouds. [[<rings of Saturn>]]
On Venus, one day, its rotation lasts longer than a year, its revolution: **243** terrestrial days against **225**.

sections.title: Why does Earth have stable seasons?

blocks.text: Without the **Moon**, the Earth's inclination would oscillate chaotically between 0° and more than 80° over millions of years. Uranus-type seasons would make the climate almost uninhabitable. The Moon acts as a **gravitational stabilizer**.
When looking for habitable s, astronomers also look at the stability of the axis. Mild and regular seasons are not a detail: they are part of the conditions for sustainable living. [[<exoplanets>]]
The seasons arise mainly from the inclination of the axis. On Uranus, they last for decades; on Mars, the oval orbit makes them asymmetrical. The Moon protects those on Earth.
